title: US product-market creative destruction passes asymmetric risk through to incumbent workers
source_unit: US administrative worker earnings, firm product-market innovation, incumbent employment, and technology-driven creative-destruction measures

observations.period: Working paper issued July 2026; US administrative data and product-market innovation exposure

denominator.unit: US administrative worker and firm observations; exact sample count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

rival_innovation_earnings_effect.unit: profit drops from rival innovations produce proportionally greater incumbent-worker earnings declines than profit gains from own-firm innovations produce gains

rival_innovation_job_destruction_effect.unit: rival-innovation profit drops change the likelihood of job destruction; exact estimate not disclosed in the abstract

top_worker_exposure.unit: top workers are significantly more exposed than the average worker

observations.method: US administrative data linking worker earnings and employment with product-market innovation and firm-profit changes; the paper also develops an endogenous-growth model with monopsonistic labor markets and worker heterogeneity.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose sample counts, effect sizes, exposure windows, or the full identification strategy. The paper is a working paper and combines empirical evidence with a model; it does not directly observe every worker's bargaining, household resources, or political response.
observations.subgroup: Incumbent workers, top workers relative to average workers, firms gaining from own innovation, and firms losing profits to rival innovation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Earnings or job losses after rival innovation may reflect firm demand, occupation mix, worker selection, or broader industry shocks rather than technology alone; upward mobility for lower-income workers does not imply that displaced workers recover quickly or equally.

observations.period: Working paper model; innovation policy and labor-income risk

denominator.unit: calibrated endogenous-growth model; no single population denominator

high_income_worker_downside.value: concentrated downside risk from creative destruction

lower_income_worker_upward_mobility.value: innovation increases upward mobility for lower-income workers

innovation_policy_welfare.value: welfare consequences depend on the asymmetric distribution of earnings risk and mobility

observations.method: Endogenous-growth model with monopsonistic labor markets and heterogeneous workers calibrated to the empirical asymmetry and earnings-risk distribution.
observations.uncertainty: Model results depend on calibration, functional forms, labor-market frictions, and how innovation exposure maps to worker outcomes; they do not establish that any specific innovation policy improves welfare in a named place or industry.
observations.subgroup: Modeled high-income and lower-income workers facing different innovation exposure and mobility paths.
observations.counterinterpretation: A worker's ability to move upward may depend on geography, credentials, care, discrimination, savings, and local demand; aggregate upward mobility can coexist with durable losses for displaced incumbents.

related_sources.claim: US firm wage-setting norms and real-wage losses during 2021–2024.
US worker and firm heterogeneity in labor-supply elasticity and modeled wage markdowns.

boundary: This record adds a US product-market-to-worker-risk mechanism. It does not report the abstract's omitted effect sizes, establish causal technology exposure for every worker, measure household hardship, bargaining or voice, or show whether mobility and policy responses restore earnings after job destruction.
